explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, the Philistines. The writer says war broke out with them at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4). That answer is sitting right there in the first verse.

Not the Moabites this time, friend. The text says war broke out with the Philistines at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4). Moab doesn't show up in this passage. The Philistines are the ones on this battlefield.

Not the ones at Gezer, friend. The text says the war was with the Philistines (1 Chronicles 20:4). The Edomites don't show up anywhere in this passage. I once grabbed the cookie cutter next to the one I wanted, so no shame here.
True! Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Sippai at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4). Sippai was a descendant of the Rephaim. The text says the Philistines were subdued.

This one is actually true, friend. The text says Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Sippai, a descendant of the Rephaim, at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4). The verse says just that. Sometimes the plain answer is just the plain answer.

Subdued is right. After Sippai was killed, the Philistines were subdued (1 Chronicles 20:4). That means they were brought low and their fight was held down. Think of dough after a good press, all the puff gone out of it.

Victorious would flip the whole story, friend. The text says the Philistines were subdued (1 Chronicles 20:4). Sippai fell, and Israel came out on top at Gezer. The Philistines don't get a victory lap here.
The text doesn't mention any reward, friend. It says the Philistines were subdued (1 Chronicles 20:4). That's a very different thing from getting a prize.
Yes! Lahmi was the brother of Goliath the Gittite (1 Chronicles 20:5). Elhanan son of Jair is the one who killed Lahmi. Now that's a famous name to find in this verse.

Og is a good pick, friend. He was king of Bashan, the only one left of the remnant of the Rephaim (Deuteronomy 3:11), so I see why you reached for him. The text says Lahmi was the brother of Goliath the Gittite (1 Chronicles 20:5). Og isn't named in this passage.

Sisera was a commander in the book of Judges (Judges 4:2), and he isn't named in this passage. The text says Lahmi was the brother of Goliath the Gittite (1 Chronicles 20:5). I'd need a bigger apron to keep all these warriors straight.

explanations.answer: Six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot
explanations.explanation: That's it! The man had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot (1 Chronicles 20:6). The text also says he was a man of great stature. It adds that he too was descended from Rapha.

explanations.answer: A bronze coat of armor weighing five thousand shekels
explanations.explanation: That's Goliath's armor, friend. The text about him says the coat of mail weighed five thousand shekels of bronze (1 Samuel 17:5). The man at Gath is different. His thing was six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot (1 Chronicles 20:6).

explanations.answer: An iron bed nine cubits long and four cubits wide
explanations.explanation: That bed belongs to Og king of Bashan, whose iron bed was nine cubits long and four cubits wide (Deuteronomy 3:11). Great pick for a big-person detail, but it's a different story. The man at Gath had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot (1 Chronicles 20:6). Nobody mentions his furniture.
Twenty-four, that's it! Six fingers on each hand is twelve, and six toes on each foot is another twelve (1 Chronicles 20:6). Add them up and the text says "…twenty-four in all." Good math, friend.

Close, but two short. Six fingers on each hand is twelve, and six toes on each foot is twelve more. The text says "…twenty-four in all." (1 Chronicles 20:6) Good guess, friend, and easy to be off by a little.
A little too generous, friend. Six fingers on each hand is twelve, and six toes on each foot is twelve more. The text says "…twenty-four in all." (1 Chronicles 20:6) Easy to be off by a little.

Yes! When the man at Gath taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei killed him (1 Chronicles 20:7). Shimei was David's brother, so Jonathan is David's nephew. A family member took care of it, and that's the whole story.

Abishai, Zeruiah's son, was one of David's fighting men, so I see why you picked him. He killed three hundred men with his spear in 1 Chronicles 11:20. At Gath, though, it was Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei who killed the man (1 Chronicles 20:7).

Benaiah, Jehoiada's son, is another of David's mighty men, and a strong pick. He's known for killing a lion in a pit on a snowy day (1 Chronicles 11:22). The man who taunted Israel at Gath fell to Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei (1 Chronicles 20:7).
David is right, friend. The text says these descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). Those two go together in that line, David and his servants.

Servants, yes. The text says they fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). Sibbecai, Elhanan and Jonathan are each named in this passage as killing one of these men. David and his servants, together, are who the verse names.
Saul isn't in this passage, friend. The text says they fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). Saul's name doesn't appear in that line.

Priests aren't named in this passage, friend. The text says the descendants of Rapha fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). The fighters named are Sibbecai, Elhanan and Jonathan, the son of David's brother Shimei (1 Chronicles 20:7).

Joab was David's army commander, so he's a good guess. He's the one who led the attack on Rabbah in 1 Chronicles 20:1. In verse 8, though, the text says they fell at the hands of David and his servants (1 Chronicles 20:8). Joab's name isn't in that line.
